tool.name: Database design
tool.tagline: Model data, choose keys and indexes, and reason about transactions and scale
tool.description: Database design is the craft of turning a problem domain into tables, keys, constraints and indexes that stay correct and fast as data grows. It also covers how databases keep data safe under concurrency (transactions, isolation, MVCC) and how systems scale out with replication and sharding. These ideas apply to every relational database and shape when a NoSQL store is the better fit.

concepts.name: Entities, attributes and relationships
concepts.summary: Describe a domain as entities with attributes and the relationships between them before writing any SQL.
concepts.why: A clear conceptual model is what keeps a schema small, correct and easy to change later.
concepts.body:
**Data modelling** is deciding what your system needs to remember and how those facts relate. Start away from SQL, in the language of the domain: an online shop has *customers*, *products* and *orders*. These are **entities** — things with identity that you store many of. Each has **attributes** (a customer has an email and a name) and they are connected by **relationships** (a customer *places* orders; an order *contains* products).

A useful way to work is in three passes:

- **Conceptual**: entities and relationships, often drawn as an entity-relationship (ER) diagram. No types, no tables.
- **Logical**: tables, columns, keys and constraints for a relational model, still independent of a particular product.
- **Physical**: types, indexes, partitioning and settings for the actual database you run.

Good questions while modelling: what uniquely identifies this thing? Can this attribute have several values (then it is probably its own entity)? Does this fact belong to the entity or to the relationship? The price a customer actually paid belongs to the order line, not the product, because the product's price changes later.

Model the facts, not the screens. A UI shows a "customer dashboard", but the database stores customers, orders and payments; the dashboard is a query. Schemas built around screens end up duplicating data and break when the UI changes.
takeaways: Entities have identity, attributes describe them, relationships connect them
Work conceptual, then logical, then physical
Store facts where they belong: the paid price lives on the order line
pitfalls: Designing tables to mirror UI screens instead of the domain's facts.

quiz.q: Where should the price a customer paid for an item be stored?
options: On the order line for that item
It should be recomputed from the current product price
quiz.explain: The paid price is a fact of that sale and must not change when the product's list price changes later.

concepts.name: One-to-many and many-to-many
concepts.summary: Represent 1:1, 1:N and M:N relationships with foreign keys and junction tables.
concepts.why: Getting cardinality right is the most common modelling decision and the hardest to undo once data exists.
concepts.body:
Every relationship has a **cardinality**: how many rows on each side can be linked.

- **One-to-many (1:N)**: a customer has many orders, each order has one customer. Put a foreign key on the *many* side: `orders.customer_id`. This is by far the most common shape.
- **Many-to-many (M:N)**: a student takes many courses and a course has many students. Relational tables can't hold a list in a column, so you add a **junction table** (also called an associative or join table) with a foreign key to each side. Its primary key is usually the pair, which also prevents duplicates.
- **One-to-one (1:1)**: a user has at most one profile. Use a foreign key that is also `UNIQUE` (or make the child's primary key the foreign key). Often 1:1 tables are simply merged, unless one side is optional, large or has different access rules.

Junction tables frequently grow attributes of their own: an enrollment has a grade and an enrolled date. When that happens the relationship has become an entity, which is fine — give it a name from the domain.

Optionality matters too. `NOT NULL` on the foreign key says "every order must have a customer"; a nullable one says the link is optional. Decide deliberately, because the constraint is what stops orphaned or half-linked data.
takeaways: 1:N: foreign key on the many side
M:N: junction table with a composite primary key
1:1: a foreign key that is also unique (or the primary key)
pitfalls: Storing comma-separated ids in a column instead of a junction table.

quiz.q: Students take many courses and courses have many students. How is this modelled?
options: A junction table with a foreign key to each
A single table with every student-course pair as columns
quiz.explain: M:N needs a junction table; each row links one student to one course.

concepts.name: Natural, surrogate and composite keys
concepts.summary: Choose primary keys: natural vs surrogate, composite keys, and why you still need unique constraints.
concepts.why: The key you pick is referenced everywhere, so changing it later touches every related table.
concepts.body:
A **candidate key** is any minimal set of columns that uniquely identifies a row. You pick one as the **primary key**; the others should still be enforced with `UNIQUE` constraints.

- A **natural key** comes from the domain: an ISO country code, an ISBN, an email. It is meaningful but can change (people change emails) or turn out not to be unique.
- A **surrogate key** is generated by the database: an identity integer or a UUID. It never changes and is cheap to reference, so most application tables use one.
- A **composite key** spans several columns; junction tables are the classic case: `(student_id, course_id)`.

The important rule: a surrogate key doesn't remove the need to enforce the natural one. If emails must be unique, declare `UNIQUE (email)`, otherwise two rows for the same person will appear the first time a form is double-submitted.

Integer vs UUID: `bigint` identities are small and index-friendly; UUIDs can be generated anywhere (clients, other services) and don't reveal row counts. Random UUIDv4 values scatter inserts across a B-tree index; time-ordered UUIDv7 keeps inserts mostly sequential and is now the usual choice when you want UUIDs.

Keep keys immutable. If a value can change, don't make it the primary key.
takeaways: Primary key = the chosen candidate key; enforce the others with UNIQUE
Surrogate keys are stable; natural keys carry meaning but may change
Prefer bigint identities or time-ordered UUIDs over random UUIDs for hot inserts
pitfalls: Adding a surrogate id and forgetting the UNIQUE constraint on the real-world key.

quiz.q: A users table has a surrogate id primary key. Emails must be unique. What else do you need?
options: Nothing, the primary key guarantees uniqueness
quiz.explain: The primary key only makes id unique; uniqueness of email has to be declared separately.

concepts.name: Constraints encode business rules
concepts.summary: Use NOT NULL, CHECK, UNIQUE and foreign keys so the database itself rejects invalid data.
concepts.why: Application checks get bypassed by scripts, bugs and race conditions; constraints don't.
concepts.body:
A schema is not just storage; it is a set of rules every row must obey. Declaring those rules as **constraints** means the database rejects bad data no matter which code path wrote it — the web app, a cron job, or a person in a SQL console.

- `NOT NULL` for every column that must always have a value. Make nullable the exception you justify.
- `CHECK` for row-level rules: `quantity > 0`, `ends_at > starts_at`, `status IN ('new','paid','shipped')`.
- `UNIQUE` for "only one of these": one account per email, one active cart per user (with a partial unique index in databases that support it).
- **Foreign keys** so references always point to existing rows; choose `ON DELETE` behaviour (`RESTRICT`, `CASCADE`, `SET NULL`) deliberately.

Why not validate only in the application? Because two requests can both check "is this email free?" and both insert. Only a unique constraint closes that race: one insert succeeds, the other gets an error you can turn into a friendly message.

Constraints also document intent. A new developer reading `CHECK (discount BETWEEN 0 AND 100)` learns a business rule without hunting through code. The cost is small: a little work on each write, which is almost always worth it.
concepts.code:
CREATE TABLE booking (
    id        bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    room      int  NOT NULL,
    starts_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
    ends_at   timestamptz NOT NULL,
    status    text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'new'
              CHECK (status IN ('new', 'confirmed', 'cancelled')),
    CHECK (ends_at > starts_at)
);
INSERT INTO booking (room, starts_at, ends_at)
VALUES (101, '2026-05-01 14:00+00', '2026-05-01 12:00+00');
-- ERROR: new row for relation "booking" violates check constraint
--        "booking_check"
takeaways: Constraints are enforced for every writer, not just your app
Only a UNIQUE constraint safely prevents concurrent duplicates
Default to NOT NULL; allow NULL only when 'unknown' is a real state
pitfalls: Relying on a SELECT-then-INSERT check in code to prevent duplicates.

quiz.q: Two requests check that a username is free and both try to insert it at the same moment. What reliably stops the duplicate?
options: Wrapping each request's SELECT in a transaction
quiz.explain: Only the unique constraint is enforced atomically by the database; the second insert fails.

concepts.name: Normalisation: 1NF to BCNF
concepts.summary: Remove redundancy with the normal forms so each fact is stored exactly once.
concepts.why: Redundant data drifts out of sync; normalisation is the systematic way to prevent update anomalies.
concepts.body:
**Normalisation** organises tables so each fact is stored in one place. When a fact is copied into many rows, an update that misses one copy leaves the data contradicting itself — an **update anomaly**.

The normal forms are a checklist, each building on the last:

- **1NF**: every column holds a single value; no repeating groups like `phone1, phone2, phone3` or comma-separated lists. Multi-valued attributes become their own table.
- **2NF**: no column depends on only *part* of a composite key. In `order_line(order_id, product_id, product_name)`, `product_name` depends on `product_id` alone, so it belongs in `product`.
- **3NF**: no column depends on another non-key column. If `employee` stores `dept_id` and `dept_name`, then `dept_name` depends on `dept_id`, not on the employee — move it to `department`.
- **BCNF**: every determinant is a candidate key; a stricter 3NF that matters in rare overlapping-key cases.

The memorable summary for 3NF: every non-key column depends on "the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key".

A normalised schema has more tables and more joins, which relational databases handle very well. Aim for 3NF by default in transactional systems, and denormalise later only for a measured reason.
takeaways: Normalise so every fact lives in exactly one place
1NF: atomic values; 2NF: whole key; 3NF: nothing but the key
3NF is the sensible default for OLTP schemas
pitfalls: Treating normalisation as optional and patching inconsistencies with application code later.

quiz.q: Table order_line(order_id, product_id, quantity, product_name) has primary key (order_id, product_id). Which normal form does product_name violate?
quiz.explain: product_name depends on only part of the composite key (product_id), which is a 2NF violation.

concepts.name: OLTP vs OLAP workloads
concepts.summary: Recognise transactional and analytical workloads, because they lead to opposite design choices.
concepts.why: Most design trade-offs (normalise or not, which indexes, row or column store) depend on the workload.
concepts.body:
Before choosing a schema shape or a database, ask what the workload looks like.

**OLTP** (online transaction processing) is what applications do: many small, concurrent reads and writes that touch a few rows by key — place an order, update a profile, fetch a user's cart. It needs low latency, strong correctness under concurrency, and normalised schemas with good indexes. PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite are OLTP databases at heart.

**OLAP** (online analytical processing) is reporting and analytics: fewer queries, each scanning millions of rows and aggregating a handful of columns — revenue per region per month. It favours **column-oriented** storage (only the needed columns are read, and they compress well), denormalised **star schemas** (a central fact table plus dimension tables), and batch loading. Warehouses such as BigQuery, Snowflake, ClickHouse or DuckDB are built for this.

Mixing them hurts both: a heavy report scanning an OLTP database competes with user traffic for I/O and can hold back cleanup of old row versions. The common architecture is to run the application on an OLTP database and copy data (via replication, change data capture or batch ETL) into an analytical store.

When someone says "the database is slow", find out which kind of query is slow — the fixes are different.
takeaways: OLTP: many small keyed reads/writes, normalised, row store
OLAP: few big scans and aggregates, denormalised, column store
Keep heavy analytics off the primary OLTP database

quiz.q: Which storage layout suits queries that aggregate two columns over 500 million rows?
options: Row-oriented, because whole rows are read together
Key-value, because lookups are by key
Column-oriented, because only the needed columns are read
quiz.explain: A column store reads and decompresses only the referenced columns, which is ideal for wide scans.

concepts.name: Transactions and ACID
concepts.summary: Group statements into all-or-nothing transactions and understand what atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability promise.
concepts.why: ACID is what lets you reason about money transfers, stock counts and any multi-step change safely.
concepts.body:
A **transaction** groups statements so they succeed or fail together. The classic example is a transfer: debit one account and credit another. If the system crashes between the two, you must not lose or create money.

**ACID** names the guarantees:

- **Atomicity**: all statements commit, or none do. On error or `ROLLBACK`, every change is undone.
- **Consistency**: a transaction takes the database from one valid state to another — every constraint holds at commit. (This is the database's part; your business logic must also be correct.)
- **Isolation**: concurrent transactions don't see each other's half-done work. How strictly this holds depends on the **isolation level**.
- **Durability**: once `COMMIT` returns, the change survives a crash, because it was written to a durable log first.

Keep transactions short. A transaction that stays open while waiting for a user or an HTTP call holds locks and old row versions, which blocks other work and bloats storage.

Every statement runs in a transaction even if you don't write `BEGIN`: in autocommit mode each statement is its own transaction. Explicit transactions are for when several statements must stand or fall together.
takeaways: A transaction is all-or-nothing
ACID = atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability
Keep transactions short; never wait on users or the network inside one
pitfalls: Doing related writes in separate autocommitted statements and hoping nothing fails in between.

quiz.q: Which ACID property guarantees that a committed transfer is still there after a power failure?
quiz.explain: Durability: committed changes are on durable storage (via the write-ahead log) before COMMIT returns.

concepts.name: What an index is and what it costs
concepts.summary: An index is a separate sorted structure that turns full scans into lookups, at a cost on every write.
concepts.why: Most slow queries are missing an index, and most bloated databases have indexes nobody uses.
concepts.body:
Without an index, finding `WHERE email = 'a@b.com'` means reading every row: a **sequential scan**, fine for a thousand rows and painful for a hundred million. An **index** is a separate data structure, kept in sync with the table, that maps column values to row locations so the database can jump straight to matching rows.

An index is a trade-off:

- Reads that filter, join or sort on the indexed columns get much faster.
- Every `INSERT`, `DELETE`, and every `UPDATE` of indexed columns must also update the index, so writes get slower.
- Indexes take disk space and memory (cache).

What to index, in practice:

- Primary keys and unique constraints (databases index these automatically).
- Foreign-key columns used in joins and in `ON DELETE` checks — many databases do *not* index these automatically.
- Columns in frequent, selective `WHERE` clauses.

**Selectivity** matters: an index on a column where 90% of rows share one value rarely helps, because reading most of the table through an index is slower than scanning it. The query planner decides whether to use an index based on statistics, so an index existing doesn't mean it will be used.

Add indexes for real queries you have measured, and periodically drop ones that are never used.
takeaways: Indexes speed up reads on their columns and slow down writes
Index foreign keys and selective, frequently filtered columns
The planner may ignore an index when a scan is cheaper
pitfalls: Indexing every column just in case, which slows every write and wastes cache.

quiz.q: A status column has the value 'active' in 95% of rows. Why might an index on it not be used for WHERE status = 'active'?
options: Indexes don't work on text columns
The index must be rebuilt first
Reading 95% of rows through the index costs more than scanning the table
Only primary keys can be used for filtering
quiz.explain: For low-selectivity predicates a sequential scan is cheaper, so the planner chooses it.

concepts.name: B-tree indexes
concepts.summary: How B-trees keep keys sorted in shallow, balanced trees so equality, range and ORDER BY queries are fast.
concepts.why: B-trees are the default index in almost every database; knowing their shape explains which queries they help.
concepts.body:
A **B-tree** (in practice a B+tree) stores keys in sorted order in fixed-size pages. Internal pages hold separator keys and pointers to child pages; leaf pages hold the keys with pointers to rows and are linked to their neighbours. Because each page holds hundreds of keys, the tree is very **shallow**: three or four levels cover hundreds of millions of rows, so a lookup reads only a few pages, and the upper levels are almost always cached.

Because the keys are sorted, one B-tree supports many operations:

- equality: `WHERE id = 7`
- ranges: `WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01' AND created_at < '2026-02-01'`
- prefix matches: `WHERE name LIKE 'Ana%'` (with a suitable collation or operator class)
- sorting: `ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20` can read the index in order and stop early
- `MIN`/`MAX` of the indexed column

It does *not* help with `LIKE '%ana%'` (no fixed prefix) or with a function of the column (`WHERE lower(email) = ...`) unless you index that expression.

The tree stays balanced as rows are inserted by splitting full pages. Inserting increasing keys (identities, timestamps, UUIDv7) appends to the rightmost leaf, which is cache-friendly; random keys (UUIDv4) cause splits all over the tree and a larger working set.
takeaways: B-trees are sorted, balanced and shallow: lookups read only a few pages
They serve equality, ranges, prefix matches and ORDER BY ... LIMIT
Sequential keys insert cheaply; random keys spread writes across the tree
pitfalls: Expecting a B-tree to speed up LIKE '%text%' or a function applied to the column.

quiz.q: Which query can a B-tree index on created_at NOT help with?
quiz.explain: A function of the column doesn't match the index order; you would need an expression index on extract(dow ...).

concepts.name: Hash indexes
concepts.summary: Hash indexes map a hash of the key to rows: only equality lookups, but compact and constant-time.
concepts.why: Knowing when hashing beats sorting (and when it can't help) clarifies how every index type is a trade-off.
concepts.body:
A **hash index** applies a hash function to the key and stores row pointers in buckets addressed by that hash. A lookup computes the hash and reads one bucket, so cost doesn't grow with the size of the index the way tree depth does (though in practice B-tree depth grows very slowly too).

The price is that hashing destroys order. A hash index can answer only **equality**: `WHERE token = '...'`. It cannot do ranges, prefix matches, `ORDER BY` or `MIN`/`MAX`, and it usually can't enforce uniqueness or cover multiple columns.

Where they show up:

- In **PostgreSQL**, `CREATE INDEX ... USING hash` exists and has been crash-safe since version 10. It can be smaller than a B-tree for long keys (it stores only the 4-byte hash), useful for equality lookups on long strings like URLs. Still, B-tree is the default for good reason and is rarely much slower.
- **MySQL InnoDB** builds B-trees even if you write `USING HASH`; its "adaptive hash index" is an internal cache on top of B-trees. The MEMORY engine supports real hash indexes.
- Hashing is everywhere internally: **hash joins** build an in-memory hash table of one input, and key-value stores and distributed systems use hashing to place keys on nodes.

Rule of thumb: use B-tree unless you have measured that a hash index is smaller or faster for a pure-equality workload.
takeaways: Hash indexes support only equality lookups
They store the hash, so they can be small for long keys
B-tree stays the default; hashing matters more inside joins and sharding
pitfalls: Choosing a hash index and later needing ORDER BY or range queries on the same column.

quiz.q: Which query could a hash index on email serve?
quiz.explain: Hashing preserves only equality; ranges, prefixes and ordering need a sorted structure.

concepts.name: Composite and covering indexes
concepts.summary: Order columns in multi-column indexes by how queries filter and sort, and cover queries to skip the table.
concepts.why: One well-designed composite index often replaces several single-column ones and serves a hot query alone.
concepts.body:
A **composite index** on `(a, b, c)` sorts rows by `a`, then by `b` within equal `a`, then by `c`. Like a phone book sorted by last name then first name, it helps queries that constrain a **leftmost prefix** of the columns:

- `WHERE a = 1` and `WHERE a = 1 AND b = 2` use it well.
- `WHERE b = 2` alone generally can't use it efficiently (some engines can skip-scan, but don't count on it).
- `WHERE a = 1 ORDER BY b` reads rows already sorted — no sort step.

Rules of thumb for column order: put columns compared with **equality** first, then the column used for a **range** or `ORDER BY` last. Once a range appears (`b > 5`), columns after it can't narrow the search further.

A **covering index** contains every column the query needs, so the database answers from the index without visiting the table (an *index-only scan*). PostgreSQL and SQL Server let you add non-key payload columns with `INCLUDE`; in MySQL InnoDB every secondary index implicitly contains the primary key.

Composite indexes also make some single-column indexes redundant: `(user_id, created_at)` already serves `WHERE user_id = ?`. Before adding an index, check whether an existing one with the same leading column covers it.
takeaways: Composite indexes serve queries on a leftmost prefix of their columns
Equality columns first, then the range or ORDER BY column
Covering indexes let the database skip the table entirely
pitfalls: Creating (created_at, user_id) for a query that filters user_id = ? and sorts by created_at.

quiz.q: An index exists on (country, city, created_at). Which WHERE clause uses it most effectively?
quiz.explain: Only this one constrains the leftmost columns of the index in order.

concepts.name: How the query planner chooses a plan
concepts.summary: Read execution plans: scans, join algorithms, row estimates and why the planner picks one plan over another.
concepts.why: You can't tune a query you can't read the plan of; EXPLAIN is the main tool for database performance work.
concepts.body:
SQL says *what* you want, not *how* to get it. The **query planner** (optimizer) enumerates possible plans — which index or scan to use, which order to join tables, which join algorithm — estimates the cost of each from **table statistics**, and runs the cheapest.

The building blocks you'll see in a plan:

- **Scans**: sequential scan (read everything), index scan (follow index to rows), index-only scan, bitmap scan (collect row locations from an index, then read pages in order).
- **Joins**: *nested loop* (for each outer row, look up matches — great when the outer side is small and the inner side indexed), *hash join* (build a hash table of the smaller input, probe with the other — great for large unsorted inputs and equality joins), *merge join* (walk two sorted inputs together).
- **Sort**, **aggregate**, **limit** nodes on top.

`EXPLAIN` shows the chosen plan with **estimated** rows and cost; `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` actually runs the query and adds **actual** rows and timings. The single most useful thing to look for is a big gap between estimated and actual rows: the planner chose based on a wrong guess. Fixes include refreshing statistics (`ANALYZE`), adding a missing index, rewriting a predicate so it can use an index, or extended statistics for correlated columns.

Plans change as data grows, so a query that was fast at launch can flip to a different plan later.
takeaways: The planner picks the cheapest plan using estimated row counts
Nested loop for small outer + indexed inner; hash join for big equality joins
Compare estimated vs actual rows in EXPLAIN ANALYZE to find bad plans
pitfalls: Running EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a data-modifying query outside a rolled-back transaction: it really executes.

quiz.q: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows estimated rows=5 but actual rows=400000 on a join input. What is the most likely root cause of a slow plan?
options: Stale or insufficient statistics led to a bad plan choice
The query has too many columns
quiz.explain: The planner chose its strategy for 5 rows; with 400000 a different join or scan would be far cheaper.

concepts.name: Denormalisation on purpose
concepts.summary: Duplicate or precompute data deliberately for read performance, and keep the copies correct.
concepts.why: Real systems denormalise; doing it on purpose with a sync strategy is what separates a design from a mess.
concepts.body:
**Denormalisation** stores redundant or derived data to make reads cheaper: a `comment_count` on posts, a customer's name copied onto invoices, a precomputed daily totals table. It trades write complexity and consistency risk for fewer joins and less computation at read time.

Denormalise when you have a **measured** read problem that indexes and query tuning didn't solve, or when the copy is semantically a snapshot rather than a duplicate. That second case is important: an invoice *should* keep the billing address as it was when issued, so copying it isn't redundancy at all — it is a different fact.

Common techniques:

- **Counters and aggregates** kept on the parent row (`posts.comment_count`).
- **Summary or rollup tables** refreshed periodically, or materialized views.
- **Embedding** a few columns from a related table to avoid a hot join.
- **Star schemas** in analytics, where dimension data is deliberately flattened.

Every copy needs a plan to stay correct: update it in the same transaction as the source, use a trigger, or accept staleness and recompute on a schedule. Also have a way to rebuild it from the source of truth, because drift will happen. Counters updated by many concurrent writers can become lock hot spots; batching or periodic recomputation can be better than incrementing on every write.
takeaways: Denormalise for a measured read problem, not by default
Snapshots (invoice addresses) are facts, not redundancy
Every copy needs a sync strategy and a rebuild path
pitfalls: Adding a cached column with no code path that keeps it updated on every write.

quiz.q: Which is NOT really denormalisation but a separate fact?
options: The shipping address copied onto an order when it ships
A customer's name copied onto every log row for speed
quiz.explain: The address at shipping time is a historical fact of the order and must not follow later changes.

concepts.name: Isolation levels and anomalies
concepts.summary: Read uncommitted to serializable: which anomalies each level allows and what your database actually defaults to.
concepts.why: Most concurrency bugs in business logic are anomalies the chosen isolation level permits.
concepts.body:
Perfect isolation (every transaction behaves as if it ran alone) costs throughput, so SQL defines weaker **isolation levels** by the **anomalies** they allow:

- **Dirty read**: seeing another transaction's uncommitted changes.
- **Non-repeatable read**: reading the same row twice and getting different values because someone committed in between.
- **Phantom read**: re-running a query and getting new rows that match.
- **Lost update**: two transactions read a value, both write back a modified copy, and one write silently wins.
- **Write skew**: two transactions read overlapping data, each makes a decision based on it, and together they break a rule (two doctors both go off call because each saw the other on call).

The standard levels, weakest to strongest: **Read Uncommitted**, **Read Committed**, **Repeatable Read**, **Serializable**. Real databases differ: PostgreSQL defaults to Read Committed and never allows dirty reads; its Repeatable Read is snapshot isolation (no phantoms, but write skew possible); its Serializable detects dangerous patterns and aborts one transaction. MySQL InnoDB defaults to Repeatable Read; SQLite is serializable.

Practical patterns: use atomic statements (`SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock > 0`), lock the rows you'll update (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`), or run at Serializable and **retry** transactions that fail with a serialization error.
takeaways: Isolation levels are defined by which anomalies they allow
Know your default: PostgreSQL Read Committed, MySQL Repeatable Read
Prefer atomic updates or row locks; at Serializable, retry on failure
pitfalls: Read-then-write in application code at Read Committed, causing lost updates under load.

quiz.q: Two transactions each read the on-call list, see the other doctor on call, and each removes themselves. What anomaly is this?
quiz.explain: Each transaction's decision was valid on its snapshot, but together they violate the rule: that is write skew.

concepts.name: Common modelling patterns
concepts.summary: Soft deletes, history tables, polymorphic links, enums and EAV: when each pattern helps and what it costs.
concepts.why: These patterns appear in nearly every product schema, and each has a well-known trap.
concepts.body:
A few recurring problems and their usual solutions:

- **Soft delete**: mark rows `deleted_at` instead of removing them, for undo and audit. Cost: every query must filter it out, and unique constraints must ignore deleted rows (use a partial unique index `WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`). Often an archive table is cleaner.
- **History / audit**: keep previous versions in a `*_history` table with `valid_from`/`valid_to`, written by a trigger or by the application. Lets you answer "what was the price on March 3rd?".
- **Status and enums**: a lookup table or a `CHECK (status IN (...))` keeps values valid; a lookup table is easier to extend and can carry labels.
- **Polymorphic association**: a comment that can belong to a post *or* a photo. The tempting `(commentable_type, commentable_id)` pair can't have a foreign key. Safer: separate nullable foreign keys with a `CHECK` that exactly one is set, or a separate junction table per parent type.
- **Entity-attribute-value (EAV)**: rows of `(entity, attribute, value)` for arbitrary fields. Flexible, but you lose types, constraints and readable queries. A `JSON` column for genuinely free-form attributes is usually better, with real columns for anything you filter on.
- **Trees**: an adjacency list (`parent_id`) queried with recursive CTEs covers most hierarchies.

Choose the pattern that keeps the database able to enforce your rules.
takeaways: Soft deletes need filtered queries and partial unique indexes
Polymorphic links: separate FKs plus a CHECK keep referential integrity
Prefer JSON columns to EAV for free-form attributes
pitfalls: A (type, id) polymorphic pair with no foreign key, which silently accumulates orphans.

quiz.q: Why is (commentable_type, commentable_id) risky for polymorphic comments?
options: No foreign key can enforce that the referenced row exists
quiz.explain: A foreign key must reference one table, so the database can't check that the target exists.

concepts.name: Locking vs MVCC
concepts.summary: How databases implement isolation: lock-based concurrency control versus multi-version snapshots.
concepts.why: Explains why readers don't block writers in modern databases, and where blocking and deadlocks still happen.
concepts.body:
There are two broad ways to keep concurrent transactions isolated.

**Lock-based concurrency control** (classic two-phase locking) makes transactions take shared locks to read and exclusive locks to write, holding them until commit. It is simple to reason about, but readers and writers block each other and **deadlocks** — A waits for B while B waits for A — must be detected and one victim aborted.

**MVCC** (multi-version concurrency control) keeps several versions of a row. A write creates a new version instead of overwriting; each transaction reads from a **snapshot**, seeing the versions that were committed when its snapshot was taken. Result: **readers never block writers and writers never block readers**. PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, Oracle and SQL Server (with snapshot isolation) all use MVCC.

MVCC doesn't remove locks entirely. Two transactions updating the *same row* still conflict: the second waits for the first to commit or roll back. Explicit row locks (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) and table locks taken by schema changes still exist, so deadlocks still happen — usually because transactions lock the same rows in different orders. Lock rows in a consistent order (for example by id) to avoid them.

MVCC's cost is garbage: old versions must be cleaned up once no snapshot needs them (VACUUM in PostgreSQL, purge of undo logs in InnoDB). Long-running transactions hold back that cleanup and cause bloat.
takeaways: MVCC: writes create new versions; reads use a snapshot
Readers and writers don't block each other; two writers to one row do
Lock rows in a consistent order to avoid deadlocks
pitfalls: Leaving transactions open for minutes, which blocks MVCC cleanup and causes bloat.

quiz.q: Under MVCC, transaction A has updated row 7 but not committed. What happens when B runs a plain SELECT of row 7?
options: B sees the last committed version immediately
quiz.explain: Readers use their snapshot of committed versions and don't wait for writers.

concepts.name: Replication
concepts.summary: Copy data to other nodes for availability and read scaling: leader-follower, sync vs async, and replica lag.
concepts.why: Every production database runs with replicas, and replica lag causes real, confusing bugs.
concepts.body:
**Replication** keeps copies of the data on several machines. Reasons: survive a machine failure (**high availability**), spread read traffic across **read replicas**, and keep copies in other regions.

The common setup is **leader-follower** (primary-replica): all writes go to one leader, which ships its change log (PostgreSQL's WAL, MySQL's binlog) to followers that replay it. Alternatives are **multi-leader** (several nodes accept writes and must resolve conflicts) and **leaderless** quorum systems like Cassandra and DynamoDB.

The key choice is **synchronous vs asynchronous**:

- **Asynchronous**: the leader commits without waiting for followers. Fast, but if the leader dies, the last few committed transactions may never have reached any follower and are lost on failover.
- **Synchronous**: commit waits until at least one follower confirms. No data loss on failover, but higher latency, and writes stall if the synchronous follower is down. A common compromise is one synchronous follower plus asynchronous others.

With async replicas, reads can be stale (**replication lag**). Classic bug: a user saves their profile, the page reloads from a replica, and the change "disappears". Fixes include reading your own recent writes from the leader, or waiting until the replica has caught up to the write's log position.

Replication is not a backup: a `DROP TABLE` replicates too. You still need backups with point-in-time recovery.
takeaways: Leader-follower: writes to one node, changes streamed to replicas
Async replication can lose recent commits on failover; sync adds latency
Replica lag breaks read-your-writes; replication is not a backup
pitfalls: Sending a read to a replica right after a write and assuming it reflects that write.

quiz.q: A system uses asynchronous replication and the leader crashes. What risk does failover carry?
options: All replicas must be rebuilt from scratch
Recently committed transactions may be missing on the new leader
quiz.explain: With async replication the leader doesn't wait for followers, so the latest commits may not have been shipped.

quiz.q: Why is a replica not a substitute for backups?
options: Mistakes such as DROP TABLE replicate to the replicas too
Replicas use a different file format
quiz.explain: Replication faithfully copies destructive changes; only backups let you go back in time.

concepts.name: Partitioning and sharding
concepts.summary: Split big tables into partitions on one server, or shard data across servers, and choose a good partition key.
concepts.why: When one table or one machine is no longer enough, the partition key decides whether scaling works.
concepts.body:
**Partitioning** splits one logical table into smaller physical pieces on the *same* database server. Common schemes:

- **Range**: by date, e.g. one partition per month. Ideal for time series: queries for last week touch one partition, and dropping old data is an instant `DROP` of a partition instead of a huge `DELETE`.
- **List**: by a discrete value such as region.
- **Hash**: by a hash of a key, to spread rows evenly.

The planner skips partitions that can't match the `WHERE` clause (**partition pruning**), so queries must filter on the partition key to benefit.

**Sharding** splits data across *multiple servers*, each holding a subset of rows. It scales writes and storage beyond one machine, but adds real costs: cross-shard queries and joins are expensive, transactions across shards need coordination, and moving data when adding shards (**rebalancing**) is operationally hard.

Choosing the **shard key** is the critical decision:

- High cardinality and even distribution, to avoid **hot shards** (sharding by country puts most rows on one shard).
- Matches the access pattern, so most queries hit one shard: shard a multi-tenant SaaS by `tenant_id` so each customer's data lives together.
- Stable: a row's shard key shouldn't change.

Consistent hashing or a directory of key ranges lets you add shards without moving everything. Exhaust simpler options first — indexes, caching, read replicas, a bigger machine — because sharding is hard to undo.
takeaways: Partitioning splits a table within one server; sharding across servers
Queries must filter on the partition key to get pruning
A good shard key is high-cardinality, evenly spread and matches access patterns
pitfalls: Sharding before trying indexes, caching, replicas and vertical scaling.

quiz.q: A multi-tenant SaaS shards its database. Which shard key keeps most queries on a single shard?
quiz.explain: Nearly every query is scoped to one tenant, so tenant_id keeps a tenant's data and queries together.

concepts.name: CAP and PACELC
concepts.summary: During a network partition a distributed store must choose consistency or availability; otherwise it trades latency for consistency.
concepts.why: CAP is the vocabulary used to describe every distributed database's behaviour under failure.
concepts.body:
The **CAP theorem** concerns a data store replicated across nodes. Of three properties it can't guarantee all at once when the network fails:

- **Consistency** (here meaning linearizability): every read sees the most recent write.
- **Availability**: every request to a working node gets a non-error response.
- **Partition tolerance**: the system keeps operating when messages between nodes are lost.

Network partitions *will* happen, so P isn't optional. The real choice is what to do **during a partition**: refuse some requests to stay consistent (**CP**: e.g. a single-leader database where the side without the leader rejects writes, or etcd/ZooKeeper) or keep answering on both sides and reconcile later (**AP**: e.g. Cassandra or DynamoDB in their default eventually consistent modes).

CAP is often oversimplified. It says nothing about the normal case, and real systems offer tunable choices per request (quorum reads, strongly consistent reads). **PACELC** fills the gap: if Partitioned, choose A or C; **E**lse, choose **L**atency or **C**onsistency. Even without failures, waiting for replicas to agree costs latency, so many systems pick lower latency and weaker consistency in normal operation too.

When evaluating a database, ask concretely: what happens to writes and reads on each side of a partition, and what does a read return right after a write in normal operation?
takeaways: During a partition you choose consistency (refuse requests) or availability (serve possibly stale data)
P is not optional in a distributed system
PACELC adds the everyday trade-off: latency vs consistency
pitfalls: Describing a single-node database as 'CA' — CAP is about replicated systems under partition.

quiz.q: A replicated store keeps accepting writes on both sides of a network split and reconciles conflicts afterwards. How is it classified under CAP?
quiz.explain: It stays available during the partition at the cost of consistency, so it is AP.

concepts.name: Choosing SQL vs NoSQL
concepts.summary: Match the data model and access patterns to relational, document, key-value, wide-column or graph stores.
concepts.why: Picking a store for the wrong reasons is expensive; the right choice follows from access patterns and guarantees needed.
concepts.body:
"NoSQL" covers several different models, each optimised for something specific:

- **Relational** (PostgreSQL, MySQL): flexible queries and joins, constraints, transactions. The best default when you don't know all future queries, and modern versions handle JSON well.
- **Document** (MongoDB): self-contained JSON-like documents; great when data is read and written as a whole aggregate (an order with its lines). Cross-document relationships and transactions are weaker or costlier.
- **Key-value** (Redis, DynamoDB at heart): get/put by key at very low latency; caches, sessions, counters. You must know the key.
- **Wide-column** (Cassandra): massive write throughput across many nodes, tables designed per query, tunable consistency.
- **Graph** (Neo4j): traversals over many-hop relationships.
- **Search** (Elasticsearch, OpenSearch) and **analytical/columnar** stores for full-text and OLAP.

Questions that decide it:

- Do you know the access patterns up front? NoSQL stores usually want you to design tables per query; relational lets you query new ways later.
- Do you need multi-row transactions and constraints?
- Does the data fit one machine (with replicas)? Most applications do, for a long time.
- What does the team already operate well?

A common, sensible architecture is a relational database as the system of record, plus specialised stores (cache, search index, warehouse) fed from it. Choose NoSQL for a concrete need — scale, latency, a data shape — not because the schema feels inconvenient.
takeaways: Relational is the best default when queries will evolve
NoSQL stores are optimised for specific shapes and access patterns
System of record in SQL plus specialised stores is a common, strong design
pitfalls: Picking a schemaless store to avoid designing a schema, then reinventing constraints in code.

quiz.q: An app needs flexible ad-hoc reporting, foreign keys and multi-row transactions on a few hundred GB. What fits best?
quiz.explain: Joins, constraints, transactions and ad-hoc queries at this size are exactly what relational databases do best.

quiz.q: Which workload most clearly favours a key-value store like Redis?
options: Session lookups by session id with sub-millisecond latency
quiz.explain: Key-value stores excel at fast get/put by a known key.

concepts.name: Consistency models
concepts.summary: Linearizability, sequential, causal and eventual consistency, plus session guarantees like read-your-writes.
concepts.why: Precise consistency vocabulary is how you compare distributed databases and debug anomalies across replicas.
concepts.body:
"Consistent" means different things in different contexts. In distributed systems, a **consistency model** defines which values a read may return given the writes that happened. From strongest to weakest:

- **Linearizability** (strong consistency): the system behaves as if there were one copy, and every operation takes effect atomically at some instant between its start and end. Once a write completes, every later read sees it. Needed for locks, leader election, unique usernames. Requires coordination (consensus such as Raft or Paxos), so it costs latency.
- **Sequential consistency**: all clients see operations in the same order, consistent with each client's own order, but not necessarily real-time order.
- **Causal consistency**: operations that are causally related (a reply after the message it answers) are seen in that order everywhere; unrelated ones may be seen in different orders. Achievable while staying available during partitions.
- **Eventual consistency**: if writes stop, replicas eventually converge. Says nothing about what you read meanwhile.

Between these sit **session guarantees** that fix the most visible problems cheaply: *read-your-writes*, *monotonic reads* (never see time go backwards), *monotonic writes* and *writes-follow-reads*.

Don't confuse this with **serializability**, which is about transactions over multiple objects (isolation), whereas linearizability is about single-object recency. **Strict serializability** combines both, and is what systems like Spanner offer.
takeaways: Linearizable: behaves like a single copy in real time
Causal consistency preserves cause-and-effect order and survives partitions
Serializability (isolation) and linearizability (recency) are different guarantees
pitfalls: Assuming 'eventually consistent' bounds how stale a read can be.

quiz.q: A user posts a comment, refreshes, and the comment is missing because the read hit a lagging replica. Which guarantee was violated?
quiz.explain: A client should always see its own writes; this session guarantee is what failed.

concepts.name: Distributed transactions, sagas and outbox
concepts.summary: Keep data consistent across services and shards: two-phase commit, sagas with compensation, and the transactional outbox.
concepts.why: Once data lives in several databases, single-database ACID no longer covers a business operation.
concepts.body:
When an operation spans several databases or services (charge a card, reserve stock, create a shipment), a local transaction can't make it atomic.

**Two-phase commit (2PC)** uses a coordinator. Phase 1: every participant prepares (makes the change durable but undecided) and votes yes or no. Phase 2: the coordinator tells all to commit, or all to abort. It gives atomicity, but participants hold locks while waiting, and if the coordinator fails after prepare they are stuck **in doubt** until it recovers. Databases support it (`PREPARE TRANSACTION` in PostgreSQL, XA in MySQL), but it is rarely used across microservices.

A **saga** splits the operation into local transactions, each with a **compensating action** that semantically undoes it (refund the charge, release the reservation). If step 3 fails, run compensations for steps 2 and 1. Sagas give eventual consistency, not isolation: other requests can see intermediate states, so design for that (e.g. a `pending` status).

A recurring sub-problem is **dual writes**: update the database *and* publish an event. If you do both directly, a crash between them loses one. The **transactional outbox** fixes this: write the event into an `outbox` table in the same local transaction as the data change; a separate relay (or change data capture from the log) publishes it to the broker. Consumers must be **idempotent**, because delivery is at-least-once.
takeaways: 2PC gives atomicity across nodes but blocks when the coordinator fails
Sagas use local transactions plus compensating actions
The outbox pattern avoids lost events from dual writes; consumers must be idempotent
pitfalls: Writing to the database and then publishing to a broker in two independent steps.

quiz.q: Why does the transactional outbox pattern prevent lost events?
options: Events are sent before the transaction starts
The event row commits atomically with the data change and is published afterwards
quiz.explain: Both rows commit together in one local transaction, so the event exists if and only if the change does.

concepts.name: B-tree vs LSM-tree storage engines
concepts.summary: Compare update-in-place B-trees with log-structured merge trees: read, write and space amplification.
concepts.why: The storage engine explains why some databases ingest writes fast and others read fast, and how to tune each.
concepts.body:
Under every database is a **storage engine** that decides how data is laid out on disk. Two families dominate.

**B-tree engines** (PostgreSQL, InnoDB, SQLite) keep sorted pages and update them in place (PostgreSQL writes new row versions into heap pages, but indexes are B-trees). Reads are predictable: a few page reads per lookup. Writes may dirty a whole page to change a few bytes, plus a write-ahead log entry for crash safety, so random writes cost several disk writes each.

**LSM-tree engines** (RocksDB, Cassandra, ScyllaDB, LevelDB) buffer writes in an in-memory sorted table (memtable) plus a log, then flush it as an immutable sorted file (SSTable). Background **compaction** merges files and discards overwritten and deleted entries (tombstones). Writes are sequential and very fast. Reads may need to check the memtable and several SSTables; **Bloom filters** let most files be skipped quickly.

Engineers compare them by three amplifications:

- **Write amplification**: bytes written to disk per byte of user data (compaction rewrites data repeatedly; B-trees rewrite pages).
- **Read amplification**: disk reads per lookup (higher for LSM).
- **Space amplification**: extra disk used by stale versions (LSM before compaction, B-tree page fragmentation or MVCC bloat).

Compaction strategy (leveled vs size-tiered) trades these against each other. Choose LSM-based stores for write-heavy, append-like workloads; B-trees for read-heavy, mixed OLTP with range scans.
takeaways: B-trees update pages in place; LSM trees append and compact
LSM: fast sequential writes, more read work (mitigated by Bloom filters)
Compare engines by write, read and space amplification

quiz.q: Why are LSM-tree engines usually faster for write-heavy workloads?
options: They turn random writes into sequential appends and flushes
quiz.explain: Writes go to memory and a log, then flush as sorted files sequentially; compaction happens in the background.

quiz.q: What do Bloom filters do in an LSM engine?
options: Let reads skip SSTables that definitely don't contain a key
quiz.explain: A Bloom filter answers 'definitely not here' cheaply, cutting read amplification.

concepts.name: Zero-downtime schema changes
concepts.summary: Evolve a live schema with expand-and-contract migrations, backfills in batches and lock-aware DDL.
concepts.why: Schema changes are the most common cause of self-inflicted outages on busy databases.
concepts.body:
On a busy database a careless `ALTER TABLE` can take a lock that queues every query behind it, and a schema change deployed at the same moment as code creates a window where old code meets the new schema. The safe method is **expand and contract**:

1. **Expand**: add the new structure in a backward-compatible way — a nullable column, a new table, a new index built online.
2. **Dual write**: deploy code that writes both old and new shapes.
3. **Backfill**: copy existing data in small batches (thousands of rows per transaction) to avoid long locks, huge transactions and replica lag.
4. **Switch reads** to the new shape and verify.
5. **Contract**: stop writing the old shape, then drop it in a later release.

Lock awareness matters as much as the steps:

- Even a fast DDL statement needs a brief exclusive lock; if a long query holds a conflicting lock, the DDL waits *and blocks everyone queued behind it*. Set a short lock timeout (`SET lock_timeout = '2s'` in PostgreSQL) and retry.
- Build indexes online: `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` (PostgreSQL), `ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE` (MySQL).
- Add constraints in two steps where supported: `NOT VALID` then `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT`, so validation doesn't block writes.
- Renaming a column is a breaking change; treat it as add-new, backfill, switch, drop-old.

Every migration should be reviewed for the locks it takes and how long it runs on production-sized data.
concepts.code:
-- Rename users.fullname -> display_name without downtime (PostgreSQL)
CREATE TABLE users (id bigint PRIMARY KEY, fullname text);
SET lock_timeout = '2s';                        -- fail fast instead of queueing
ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN display_name text; -- expand (metadata only)

-- deploy code that writes both columns, then backfill in batches:
UPDATE users SET display_name = fullname
WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM users
             WHERE display_name IS NULL AND fullname IS NOT NULL LIMIT 5000);
-- ...repeat until 0 rows updated

ALTER TABLE users ADD CONSTRAINT display_name_nn
    CHECK (display_name IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID; -- no full scan under lock
ALTER TABLE users VALIDATE CONSTRAINT display_name_nn;  -- scans without blocking writes

-- switch reads, stop writing fullname, then in a later release:
ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN fullname;         -- contract
takeaways: Expand, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, contract
Set a lock timeout so DDL can't stall the whole table
Backfill in small batches; build indexes and validate constraints online
pitfalls: Renaming or dropping a column in the same deploy as the code that stops using it.

quiz.q: A quick ALTER TABLE waits for a lock held by a long-running report. What happens to new queries on that table in PostgreSQL?
options: They queue behind the waiting ALTER
quiz.explain: Lock requests queue in order, so the pending exclusive lock blocks later queries too; hence lock_timeout.
